_: latin-sounds.json — the table behind decks/Latin-Sounds-and-Spelling.folio-deck.json, read by build-latin-sounds.js. NOTHING IN IT IS COMPOSED but the labels `when`, `kind` and `name`. In `sounds`, a row's `ipa` and `like` are the 'IPA' and 'English approximation' cells of one row of the key of Wikipedia's Help:IPA/Latin at the revision in `sources.key`; `col` says which of the key's two columns of letters the row's letter stands in (Class., Eccl., or both), and that is what `when` reports: the Classical value is always first and the Church value beside it. A row with `src` phonology is instead a row of the table 'Ecclesiastical pronunciation (Italian pronunciation)' of 'Latin phonology and orthography' (its Pronunciation and English-approximation cells), used where the key has no Church row for the letter (h, ch). A `says` is a list of quotations, each a run of consecutive words of the page named beside it in `src` (key: the notes under the key's tables; phonology; declension: 'Latin declension'; conjugation: 'Latin conjugation'), with a cut marked […]. Every word is a Latin A1 headword, spelled as its card prints it, and the two transcriptions beside it are the English Wiktionary's own for that headword — the one it tags Classical Latin and the one it notes as modern Italianate Ecclesiastical — written by `python3 .claude/latin/sounds.py --fill` from the kaikki.org extraction (fetched 2026-11-27); none is typed. An ending card's table is not stored: `tableFrom` names Latin A1 cards and `blocks` the blocks of their All forms table, which build-latin-sounds.js copies, so a pattern shows only forms a card shows. `python3 .claude/latin/sounds.py --verify` fetches the four revisions and checks every cell and quotation against them. A row's `key` is what its card id is pinned to in latin-ids.json (deck lasounds): never change one.

wiktionary.title: English Wiktionary, via the kaikki.org extraction

rules.name: the classical pronunciation and the Church one
says: The charts below show the way in which the International Phonetic Alphabet (IPA) represents Classical Latin and Ecclesiastical Latin pronunciations in Wikipedia articles.
Since the late 19th and early 20th centuries, an Italianate pronunciation of Latin has grown to be accepted as a universal standard in the Catholic Church.

In Classical Latin, ⟨c g t⟩ are always pronounced hard, as [k g t]. In Ecclesiastical Latin, ⟨c g sc⟩ are pronounced as soft [tʃ dʒ ʃ] before the front vowels ⟨e i y ae oe⟩, and unstressed ⟨ti⟩ before a vowel is pronounced [tsi].

rules.name: the macron: a long vowel
says: Classical Latin has long and short vowels. If vowel length is marked, long vowels are marked with macrons, ⟨ā, ē, ī, ō, ū, ȳ⟩, and short vowels with breves, ⟨ă, ĕ, ĭ, ŏ, ŭ, y̆⟩. Ecclesiastical Latin does not distinguish between long and short vowels.

Textbooks and dictionaries usually indicate the length of vowels by putting a macron above the long vowel (less frequently, the breve is also used to mark short vowels), but it is not generally done in regular texts.

rules.name: where the stress falls
says: In words of two syllables, the stress is on the first syllable. In words of three or more syllables, the stress is on the penultimate syllable if heavy, and on the antepenultimate syllable otherwise.
Thus, a syllable is heavy if it ends in a long vowel, a diphthong, or a consonant.

rules.name: a doubled consonant
says: Geminate (double) consonants are written with a doubled letter except for /jj/ and /ww/: anus [ˈanʊs], annus [ˈannʊs].
Length is the duration of time that a particular sound is held before proceeding to the next sound in a word.

rules.name: a vowel and m at the end of a word
says: In Classical Latin, the combination of a vowel and ⟨m⟩ at the end of a word, or a vowel and ⟨n⟩ before ⟨s⟩ or ⟨f⟩, represents a long nasal vowel.

rows.when: Classical, written u in the key

says: In Classical Latin, ⟨i u⟩ represent the vowels /ɪ iː/ and /ʊ uː/, and the consonants /j/ and /w/. Between consonants or when marked with macrons or breves, ⟨i u⟩ are vowels. […] In Ecclesiastical Latin, ⟨i⟩ represents the vowel /i/, ⟨j⟩ represents the consonant /j/, ⟨u⟩ represents the vowel /u/ or (in the combinations ⟨gu su qu⟩) the consonant /w/, and ⟨v⟩ represents the fricative /v/.

[…] In Ecclesiastical Latin, ⟨i⟩ represents the vowel /i/, ⟨j⟩ represents the consonant /j/, ⟨u⟩ represents the vowel /u/ or (in the combinations ⟨gu su qu⟩) the consonant /w/, and ⟨v⟩ represents the fricative /v/.
In Ecclesiastical Latin, ⟨s⟩ between vowels is often pronounced [z].

endings.name: the cases
says: A complete Latin noun declension includes up to seven grammatical cases: nominative, vocative, accusative, genitive, dative, ablative and locative. The locative is limited to a few nouns: generally names of cities, small islands and a few other words.

The nominative and vocative are always identical in the plural. […] The dative, ablative, and locative are always identical in the plural. […] For neuter nouns, the nominative, vocative, and accusative cases are always identical.

endings.name: the first declension
says: Nouns of this declension usually end in -a in the nominative singular and are mostly feminine, e.g. via, viae f. ('road') and aqua, aquae f. ('water').

endings.name: the second declension
says: The second declension is a large group of nouns consisting of mostly masculine nouns like equus, equī ('horse') and puer, puerī ('boy') and neuter nouns like castellum, castellī ('fort').
In the nominative singular, most masculine nouns consist of the stem and the ending -us, although some end in -er, which is not necessarily attached to the complete stem.

endings.name: the third declension
says: The third declension is the largest group of nouns.
This group of nouns includes masculine, feminine, and neuter nouns.
The stem of a consonant-stem noun may be found from the genitive case by removing the ending -is.

endings.name: the fourth declension
says: The fourth declension is a group of nouns consisting of mostly masculine words such as flūctus, flūctūs m. ('wave') and portus, portūs m. ('port') with a few feminine exceptions, including manus, manūs f. ('hand') and domus, domūs f. ('house').

endings.name: the fifth declension
says: The fifth declension is a small group of nouns consisting of mostly feminine nouns like rēs, reī f. ('affair, matter, thing') and diēs, diēī m. ('day'; but f. in names of days).

endings.name: a verb's four principal parts
says: In a dictionary, Latin verbs are listed with four "principal parts" (or fewer for deponent and defective verbs), which allow the student to deduce the other conjugated forms of the verbs.
the first person singular of the present indicative active […] the present infinitive active […] the first person singular of the perfect indicative active

endings.name: the first conjugation
says: The first conjugation is characterized by the vowel ā and can be recognized by the -āre ending of the present active infinitive form.

endings.name: the second conjugation
says: The second conjugation is characterized by the vowel ē, and can be recognized by the -eō ending of the first person present indicative and the -ēre ending of the present active infinitive form

endings.name: the third conjugation
says: The third conjugation has a variable short stem vowel, which may be e, i, or u in different environments. Verbs of this conjugation end in -ere in the present active infinitive.

endings.name: the third conjugation in -iō
says: Intermediate between the third and fourth conjugation are the third-conjugation verbs with suffix –iō. These resemble the fourth conjugation in some forms.

endings.name: the fourth conjugation
says: The fourth conjugation is characterized by the vowel ī and can be recognized by the -īre ending of the present active infinitive.

endings.name: a deponent verb
says: Deponent verbs are verbs that are passive in form (that is, conjugated as though in the passive voice) but active in meaning. These verbs have only three principal parts
